plan: SAT R&W batch 56: 8 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000504..000511 (harder designs: two-part quantitative claim, alternative-explanation inference, literary inference, partly supported distractors), plus S055-09 resubmitted as revision 3. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Late quartets
passages.text: Although the composer's late string quartets were at first dismissed as ______, later critics came to hear their abrupt shifts of mood and fragmentary forms as deliberate experiments rather than as signs of a declining talent that could no longer hold a piece together.

passages.title: Seedlings and distance
passages.text:
The Janzen-Connell hypothesis holds that tree seedlings growing close to a parent tree survive less often than those farther away, because pests that specialize on that species gather near the parent. A biologist tracked seedlings of two tree species in a tropical forest and concluded that the pattern holds for species A but not for species B.
Percentage of seedlings surviving after one year
Distance from parent tree | Species A | Species B
0-5 meters | 12% | 30%
5-20 meters | 25% | 31%
more than 20 meters | 41% | 29%

passages.title: Pottery from one riverbank
passages.text: Chemical analysis shows that the clay in a distinctive style of pottery, found at sites spread across a region some 300 kilometers wide, all came from a single riverbank deposit. Some archaeologists have treated the pottery's wide distribution as evidence that the communities at those sites shared a common culture with shared craft traditions. Because the clay came from one source, however, the distribution may instead indicate that ______

passages.title: A team of specialists
passages.text: The members of the 1925 survey team included Ada Moreno, a ______ Lionel Park, a geologist; and Ruth Okafor, a photographer who later published the expedition's only surviving images.

passages.title: Conflicting findings
passages.text: The two ______ findings contradicted each other: one reported that the drug lowered blood pressure, and the other found no effect at all.

passages.title: Photography's early critics
passages.text: Many nineteenth-century critics dismissed photography as a mechanical process rather than an art. ______ the poet Charles Baudelaire wrote in 1859 that photography should be the "very humble servant" of the arts and sciences, not an art itself.

passages.title: Waiting for a treat
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1960s and 1970s, psychologist Walter Mischel ran experiments at a Stanford University nursery school.
- Children could eat one treat right away or wait to receive two treats.
- Follow-up studies found that children who waited longer tended to have higher academic achievement years later.
- A 2018 study tested this link with a larger and more diverse sample of children.
- It found that the link was much weaker and was largely explained by differences in children's family backgrounds.

passages.title: A winter crossing
passages.text: In the story, Teodor has crossed the frozen lake every winter for forty years, and the villagers treat his judgment about the ice as law. This year, however, he stops at the shore, tests the surface with his staff, and says nothing; the narrator observes that the silence of a man who has always been certain ______

passages.title: The waggle dance
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Honeybees perform a "waggle dance" that tells nestmates the direction and distance of a food source.
- The dance was decoded in the mid-twentieth century by Karl von Frisch.
- Researchers later prevented some colonies from reading dance directions.
- In some seasons, those colonies gathered about as much food as colonies that could read the dances.
- In other seasons, colonies that could read the dances gathered noticeably more food.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: deliberate experiments rather than as signs of a declining talent
candidates.explanation: The later critics treat the quartets as "deliberate," in contrast to the early view, so the early critics must have seen them as unplanned and disorganized: "haphazard."

A.rationale: "Derivative" means imitative, but the later critics answer a charge of lacking design, not of copying.

B.rationale: The fragmentary forms might seem spare, but the contrast is with "deliberate," which calls for a word meaning unplanned.

D.rationale: The quartets shift abruptly in mood, but the critics' reply concerns design, not sadness.

hints: What word is the opposite of "deliberate" here?
candidates.remember: Use the later view to predict the earlier one.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the biologist's conclusion?

choices.A: Species A survival rose sharply with distance, while species B survival was about the same at every distance.
choices.B: Species B seedlings survived at a higher rate than species A seedlings within 5 meters of the parent tree.
choices.C: Species A seedlings more than 20 meters away survived at a higher rate than species B seedlings at any distance.
choices.D: For both species, the highest survival rate occurred at a distance greater than 5 meters from the parent tree.

candidates.evidence: the pattern holds for species A but not for species B
candidates.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: survival depends on distance for species A (12% to 41%) and does not for species B (30%, 31%, 29%). Only choice A describes both parts.

B.rationale: This is true, but it compares the species at one distance and does not show how survival changes with distance for either.

C.rationale: This is true, but it says nothing about whether species B's survival depends on distance.

D.rationale: This is true, but it treats the two species alike, while the conclusion is that they differ.

hints: What would the data look like if the pattern held for one species and not the other?

strategy.explanation: Read the conclusion first, then check each species' trend.

candidates.remember: Support a two-part claim with data for both parts.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: each community in the region made its own pots from clay found near its site.
choices.B: the communities at the sites did not use the pottery for cooking or storing food.
choices.C: the riverbank deposit once supplied clay to communities across many regions.
choices.D: the pots were made near one deposit and then traded or carried to the other sites.

candidates.evidence: all came from a single riverbank deposit
candidates.explanation: If all the clay came from one place, the pots were probably made there and moved by trade or travel, which explains their spread without requiring a shared culture.

A.rationale: This contradicts the finding that all the clay came from one deposit.

B.rationale: How the pots were used does not bear on where they were made.

C.rationale: The text concerns one region; this overstates what one deposit suggests and does not offer an alternative to a shared culture.

hints: What does a single clay source suggest about where the pots were made?

strategy.explanation: Ask how one source and wide spread fit together.

candidates.remember: An alternative explanation must account for the same evidence.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Lionel Park, a geologist; and Ruth Okafor
candidates.explanation: When items in a series contain internal commas, semicolons separate the items. The semicolon after "geologist" shows that the same mark belongs after "botanist."

A.rationale: Because each item contains a comma, a comma here would make the list confusing; the semicolon used later in the series must be used here too.

C.rationale: A colon cannot separate items within a series.

D.rationale: Without punctuation, "a botanist Lionel Park" runs two items together.

hints: How is the next item in the series separated?

strategy.explanation: Look at the punctuation later in the series.

candidates.remember: Use semicolons between list items that contain commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: one reported that the drug lowered blood pressure, and the other found no effect
candidates.explanation: The findings belong to two researchers, so the plural possessive "researchers'" is correct.

B.rationale: "Researcher's" is singular, but "two" requires the plural.

C.rationale: The findings belong to the researchers, so a possessive is needed.

D.rationale: A plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.

hints: How many researchers, and do they own something?
candidates.remember: Plural possessive: add an apostrophe after the -s.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: should be the "very humble servant" of the arts and sciences
candidates.explanation: Baudelaire's remark is a strong example of the critics' dismissal described in the first sentence, so "Indeed" fits.

A.rationale: Baudelaire's view agrees with the critics' dismissal; it does not contrast with it.

B.rationale: "Nevertheless" signals an outcome despite something, but Baudelaire's remark is an instance of the dismissal.

D.rationale: Baudelaire's statement supports the first sentence rather than contrasting with it.

hints: Does Baudelaire agree or disagree with the critics?

strategy.explanation: Decide whether the second sentence supports or opposes the first.

candidates.stem: The student wants to contrast the follow-up studies' findings with the 2018 study's findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In Mischel's experiments in the 1960s and 1970s, children could eat one treat right away or wait to receive two treats.
choices.B: Follow-up studies linked waiting for a second treat to later achievement, but a larger 2018 study found the link much weaker.
choices.C: A 2018 study with a larger, more diverse sample found that differences in family background largely explained children's achievement.
choices.D: Both Mischel's follow-up studies and a 2018 study examined whether waiting for a treat was linked to later achievement.

candidates.evidence: It found that the link was much weaker
candidates.explanation: The goal requires both findings and a contrast between them. Choice B gives the follow-up studies' link and the 2018 study's weaker link, joined by "but."

A.rationale: This describes the experiment's design, not the contrast between findings.

C.rationale: This gives only the later finding and does not compare it with the follow-up studies.

D.rationale: This notes a shared topic but not how the findings differed.

hints: Which choice includes both findings and contrasts them?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for both halves of the goal.

candidates.remember: A contrast needs both sides and a signal of difference.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: proves that the ice is too thin for anyone to cross safely.
choices.B: shows that he has lost interest in the village's affairs.
choices.C: reassures the villagers that the crossing will go as usual.
choices.D: unsettles the villagers more than any warning could have.

candidates.evidence: the villagers treat his judgment about the ice as law
candidates.explanation: Because the villagers rely on Teodor's certainty, his unexpected silence would disturb them, more than a direct warning would, since it signals doubt from someone who never doubts.

A.rationale: Teodor's silence suggests doubt, but the text does not establish that the ice is unsafe.

B.rationale: Testing the ice carefully shows concern, not lack of interest.

C.rationale: A break from his usual certainty would be more likely to worry the villagers than reassure them.

hints: Why would silence from this particular man matter?

strategy.explanation: Connect the villagers' trust to his change in behavior.

candidates.remember: A change in a reliable character's behavior is itself meaningful.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize a surprising finding about the usefulness of the waggle dance. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee's waggle dance, which shows nestmates the direction and distance of food.
choices.B: Though the dance points to food, colonies unable to read it sometimes gathered about as much as normal colonies.
choices.C: In some seasons, colonies that could read the waggle dance gathered noticeably more food than others.
choices.D: Researchers prevented some honeybee colonies from reading the direction information in waggle dances.

candidates.evidence: those colonies gathered about as much food as colonies that could read the dances
candidates.explanation: The surprise is that a signal giving food locations sometimes made no difference to how much food colonies gathered. Only B pairs the dance's purpose with that result.

A.rationale: This describes the dance and its discoverer but not the surprising finding.

C.rationale: This is the expected result, not the surprising one.

D.rationale: This describes the method but not what the researchers found.

hints: What finding would be surprising, given what the dance does?

strategy.explanation: Look for a result that runs against expectation.

candidates.remember: To emphasize a surprise, pair the expectation with the result that defies it.

revision_history.reason: solver: key said colonies were unable to read the dance, but the notes say only its directions were blocked; reworded
both solvers: key dropped "about" and lacked a comparison group
revision_history.change: key reworded with "about as much as normal colonies"
